text: The weaver took over her family's workshop because orders for blankets had dried up. She learned the trade in stages, first sorting fleeces, then spinning, and at last weaving wide panels. That slow apprenticeship shaped the way she works now. She can name a fiber by touch alone, without so much as a glance at it. Industrial dyes struck her as harsh, so she colors her skeins in pots of boiled roots and bark. Every batch comes out a shade away from the last, and that unevenness draws buyers who have grown tired of uniform cloth. Demand climbed, and she had to take on an apprentice. The younger woman starts by learning to watch, because one thread pulled too tight warps the whole piece. Patience, the weaver says, is not a virtue in this room. It is a technical requirement.

units: the speaker was disappointed by a knit garment as soon as he put it on
the knit felt rough and irritating at his neck
the packaging promised a very soft material
an acquaintance who sews suggested a lukewarm wash with vinegar added
the drying had to be done flat and without wringing by hand
after that treatment the knit turned supple and downy
the speaker now recommends this method to others who are unhappy
he considers the cut bad despite the improvement in feel
no care routine in his view corrects a bad pattern
he wears the garment only at home
text: Honestly, that sweater let me down the moment I pulled it on. The knit felt scratchy, the collar rubbed at my neck, and the tag had promised a fiber as soft as a cloud. I nearly sent it straight back. Then a friend who sews told me to wash it in lukewarm water with a splash of vinegar, and to dry it flat, never wringing it out by hand. The result surprised me. The knit turned supple, almost downy, and the collar stopped prickling. I pass the trick along now to anyone who grumbles about a scratchy sweater. My objection to the cut still stands, though. The sleeves hang too long, the shoulders gape, and no amount of washing will rescue a bad pattern. Fix that and the workshop would have a decent garment at a fair price. As things stand, I wear it around the house and nowhere else.

units: the writer is writing from a place where clothes are repaired

text: I'm writing to you from the repair shop, in the gap between two fittings, because your question about shoes deserves a straight answer. You're torn between two fastenings. One buckles, the other laces. The buckle goes on in a single motion, which suits anyone who is heading out the door in a hurry. Lacing means sitting down, pulling the laces snug, checking the tension across the instep. In exchange, it holds the ankle far better than the other one does. I watch both kinds come through here. The buckle usually snaps at the rivet, and that repair runs high. Laces you can swap out for next to nothing. If you spend your days on broken, uneven ground, take the laced pair. If your days are a string of short errands, the buckle will do. Write and tell me what you decide. I've set aside a pair of each in your size.

units: the text asks what makes one material different from another

the animal fiber offers a springiness that restores the shape

the most common fiber stirs little enthusiasm because it is ordinary

text: What separates one cloth from another, if not the hand that judges it? The weaver answers by weight, the seamstress by how a piece holds its shape, the dyer by how thirstily the fiber drinks. Each is right, and each says too little. Ask them about linen and they will talk about a dry coolness, about a crease that no iron ever quite presses out. Ask about wool and they will speak of warmth that breathes, of a spring that pulls the knit back into shape. Ask about silk and they drop their voices, as though the word alone were enough. And cotton? It stirs no poetry, because it turns up everywhere and slips out of mind. There lies the riddle of these materials. They yield to description through their uses, never through what they are. Whoever handles them long enough ends up naming them by touch, eyes shut.

text: The floor manager ran through the order of operations before the run started. Cut the pieces first, he said, on cloth laid out flat and squared to the grain, or the jacket will twist in the first wash. The woman in charge of cutting answered that the pattern had been checked the day before and the templates were true. He went on. Shoulders get joined next, then the sleeves go in, and only after that does the lining go down. One of the operators asked whether the lining should be clipped in place before stitching. The answer came back flat. Clip it, check that it hangs straight, then stitch. The closure comes last of all. The cutter added that the whole thing has to be buttoned on a dress form before it ships, since a crooked line shows up on the hanger and can still be put right at that stage.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)

text: For a long stretch of history the color of a garment cost far more than the length of cloth it sat on, and that oddity shaped the whole story of dress. Stable dyes came from sea creatures, from insects, or from uncommon plants, and they were gathered only in tiny amounts. Scarcity made rank easy to read, since anyone could tell a household's standing from the depth of its reds. Rulers widened the gap by law, and forbade certain shades outright to the lowest ranks. Unable to dye anything richer, poorer workshops fell back on grays, browns, and undyed cloth, which fixed the notion of common dress as drab for generations to come. Dyes drawn from a byproduct of industry overturned that whole arrangement. Once bright color came within reach of almost anyone, hue stopped signaling wealth, and cut took over the job.

units: a new knit garment quickly fills with little balls of fiber

text: A sweater fresh off the shelf picks up little balls of fiber fast, and that wear discourages anyone who has just bought one. The cause is mechanical. Short ends work their way to the surface under rubbing, tangle together, and clump into knots that catch the eye. Long yarns, spun from well-combed fiber, slide past one another and pill far less. So the fix starts at the counter, where you look for a dense, smooth knit rather than a puffy one. After that, care matters as much as the material does. Washing the garment inside a mesh bag, with no violent spin cycle, cuts down the friction that tears the ends loose. And once the knots do show up, a fabric shaver lifts them off cleanly, as long as you spread the garment flat and never tug at it. The knit comes back looking crisp, and you can repeat the whole thing without harming it.

units: a woman living on the floor above owned two outdoor garments

the light garment gave no protection from the cold
the narrator now chooses according to the state of the sky
text: My upstairs neighbor kept two coats in one closet, and one evening she stood there and explained the difference to me. The first was heavy, cut from thick felted wool, and it sat down on the shoulders like a suit of armor. The second, made of oiled canvas, weighed almost nothing and folded down into a bag. She took the heavy one out when the wind bit, and the light one when the rain came straight down. I wanted to settle the matter, to pick the better of the two, and I was wrong to try. One night in a downpour I borrowed the wool coat. It drank the water like a sponge, and drying it out took two evenings. The other, though, left my back frozen the moment the cold set in. Now I stand at that closet and choose by the sky rather than by preference. Learning the hard way, my neighbor called it.

text: Here is the method that professional pressers use to take the wrinkles out of a shirt without scorching it. For gear, you want a padded board, a clean iron with nothing caked on the plate, and a spray bottle filled with plain water. For prep, empty out the pockets, unfasten the collar, and dampen the cloth until it goes soft under your fingers. For the order of work, begin at the collar, move on to the cuffs, then the sleeves, and finish with the back and the fronts. Narrow areas come before wide ones, since the large panels are the ones that wrinkle last. For heat, set the iron to the most delicate fiber in the garment, and test it on a hidden seam first. For storing, let the shirt cool on a hanger before you button it up, or the trapped damp will press in fresh creases.

text: The shed smelled of damp wool when the doors slid open, a little before dawn. The shearers had come in the day before, and the fleeces were waiting in downy heaps along the wall. In the first hour a sorter pulled out the soiled locks one by one, working steadily, never lifting her head. Around the middle of the session the pressed bales went off to be washed, where warm water carried away the grease. Later the dried fibers went through the carding machine, and the white cloud pouring out of it set the visitors coughing. At the end of the line a worker knitted a sample in front of the onlookers, using the first yarn off the frame. The cooperative hopes to revive a trade that buying from abroad had killed off. Nothing is settled yet. Orders are still thin, and the shearers are getting old.
